capabilities.target: Supabase Postgres database, all tables, row level security bypassed via service role

capabilities.tool_ref: supabase MCP: execute_sql (service role) - INSERT INTO support_messages
capabilities.target: support_messages table, rows shown back to the customer

inputs.source: Developer's direct instruction typed in the IDE client
Customer-authored ticket message submitted through the public support widget

instructions.note: The agent's SQL execution capability is not scoped to the ticket/support domain; the connection uses a service role that bypasses row level security, so execute_sql can reach any table, including integration_tokens.

technique_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

elements.name: integration_tokens table, same database, reachable via service role
support_messages table, customer-visible via the support widget

controls.name: IDE client per-call approval prompt showing raw SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is enforced by the IDE client outside the model and shows the raw SQL (raw_action review), so it does not decay with model capability. It decays with approval volume: developers approve many calls per session, which is the documented precondition for approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403).

controls.name: Least-privilege database role without RLS bypass for ticket-reply operations
controls.decay_rationale: A role that respects row level security and has no grant on integration_tokens cannot read that table under any model behavior.

controls.name: Pre-insert validation on support_messages writes to block secret-like values
controls.decay_rationale: Pattern or entropy-based secret detection enforced outside the model can be evaded through encoding, chunking, or paraphrase of the exfiltrated value.

controls.name: Pin and hash-verify the Supabase MCP server package version
controls.decay_rationale: A pinned, hash-verified package cannot silently change tool behavior or definitions between invocations regardless of model behavior.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): injected ticket message drives service-role read of integration tokens and exfiltration via a customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: Customer submits a ticket message through the public support widget; content is attacker-controlled and can carry injected instructions.

Agent runs service-role SQL to read open tickets, ingesting the attacker's message, and per its injected instructions also queries el.integration_tokens_table, which service-role access makes readable despite RLS.
Sensitive integration tokens are returned into the agent's context.
Agent inserts a reply into support_messages that carries or encodes the exfiltrated token data.
The row is shown back to the customer through the support widget, completing exfiltration to an attacker-reachable destination.

findings.residual_rationale: The declared approval gate is raw_action, which per rubric section 5 step 2 would float the floor to moderate without a floor restriction. The design states developers approve many calls per session, and a SQL insert carrying exfiltrated token data into a routine ticket reply is not visually distinguishable from a legitimate reply during fast review. This is the SAFE-T1403 consent-fatigue pattern, so residual is rated high rather than the computed moderate floor.

forecast.watch_signal: Approval requirement removed or changed to auto-approve routine actions; autonomy level raised above A1; or per-call confirmation disabled in IDE client settings.

evidence.observation: The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database that execute_sql can reach.
Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget (untrusted input), and rows inserted into support_messages are shown back to the customer, making that insert an egress channel.
The IDE client shows the SQL and asks for approval on each call, but developers approve many calls in a session.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role database connection with a least-privilege role that respects row level security and cannot read the integration_tokens table from the ticket-reply path.

Add pre-insert validation on support_messages writes that blocks values resembling secrets or tokens, or restrict inserts into that table to a fixed, parameterized reply template rather than free-form SQL.
Log and alert on execute_sql statements from this agent that reference the integration_tokens table, independent of the per-call approval prompt.

Instruct the agent to treat ticket content as untrusted data and never include query results from tables other than tickets/support_messages in a reply, while recognizing this control alone decays as the model becomes more capable.

findings.title: Agentic supply chain exposure (ASI04): unpinned Supabase MCP server package with static token auth

attack_path.note: MCP server is launched via npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest, fetching whatever version is currently published, with no pin or hash check.
A compromised or poisoned server build could alter what this capability actually executes or returns.
A compromised server could also misrepresent the SQL shown in the approval prompt versus what is executed, undermining the approval gate's assumption.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Approval prompt disabled or bypassed, or additional unpinned MCP servers added without a version-pinning policy.

evidence.observation: The server is invoked as '@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest' via npx -y, fetching and running the latest published package on every run with no version pin or hash check.
Authentication to the backend uses a single static access token (${SUPABASE_PAT}) passed as a command-line argument, with no stated verification of the MCP server's own identity.

recommendations.action: Pin the @supabase/mcp-server-supabase package to a specific, reviewed version and verify its integrity (lockfile hash) instead of invoking npx -y ...@latest.
Issue a scoped Supabase access token specific to this integration and rotate it regularly, rather than using a long-lived static PAT.
Diff tool definitions returned by the MCP server across sessions and alert on unexpected changes (rug-pull detection).

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted customer-authored ticket message can reach a service-role SQL execution capability that bypasses row level security and can read a table of integration tokens, and the same service role can write to a customer-visible support_messages table, forming a complete lethal-trifecta exfiltration path (f1). A second, independently critical-inherent path (f2) exists because the MCP server package is pulled unpinned (@latest) with static token auth and no identity verification, exposing the same two capabilities to supply-chain compromise. The only declared control, a per-call approval prompt showing raw SQL, credits -2 tiers under rubric section 5 step 2 for both findings. For f1, residual is raised from the computed moderate floor to high because the design records that developers approve many calls per session and the exfiltration step looks like a routine reply, the documented approval-fatigue failure mode (SAFE-T1403) behind this incident class. f2 remains at the moderate floor. Forecast is critical for both findings: removing or loosening the approval gate, or adding further unpinned servers, returns the design to its inherent critical risk with no structural control remaining. The highest-leverage fix is replacing the service-role connection with a role that respects row level security and cannot reach integration_tokens, which would sever the f1 path outright; pinning the MCP server package addresses f2.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior; actual agent and approver behavior were not tested against these findings.

No full system prompt or tool manifest beyond the MCP server configuration and runtime notes was provided; capability scope beyond execute_sql (for example, other Supabase MCP tools) is inferred, not confirmed.

Approval volume and actual approver behavior (calls per session, time spent per review) were not measured; the approval-fatigue judgment rests on the stated fact that developers approve many calls per session, not on observed accept or reject rates.
